lesson_title: Jerseys, Armbands and Till Slips: Quadrilaterals and Their Proofs
hook_text: Every square is a rectangle. Most rectangles are not squares. Get that backwards and the marks vanish.
clip_script: Quadrilaterals are one family, and every child keeps everything its parent had, then adds exactly one thing. The grandparent is just four sides. The parallelogram adds one rule: both pairs of opposite sides run parallel — like a ladder's two rails held apart by rungs. The rectangle adds square corners. The rhombus adds four equal sides. And the square, the youngest, inherits from both parents at once. Now the trap. Think of a sports team: every player wears the jersey, but only the captain wears the armband. See an armband, and you know they're on the team. See only a jersey, and you know nothing about captaincy. So every square is a rectangle — and most rectangles will never be squares. Inheritance runs downward only. Then the writing rule, in one scene: the school shop says you didn't pay for your calculator. Saying 'but I did' convinces nobody. The till slip ends it. Every line of a geometry proof is a claim, and every claim needs its receipt — the reason, written beside it. True but reasonless scores zero. And you can never present the receipt for something you haven't yet proved you own: no parallelogram properties until the shape has earned the name.
visual_style: A family tree of shapes lighting up one inheritance at a time; a team jersey with an armband sliding on; a till slip printing itself beside each line of a two-column proof.
pacing: Steady down the family tree, a sharp beat on the armband, deliberate on the receipts.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write proofs that actually collect their marks.
